title: How to Improve the Guided Practice in Your Lessons
author: Trudy Mayo
summary: Trudy Mayo tackles the 'We Do' phase of explicit teaching — guided practice — arguing it's one of the hardest parts of a lesson to execute well because, unlike modelling or independent practice, there's no fixed script to follow. She explains that guided practice demands teachers observe, respond, and adjust in real time since different classes and groups of students require different numbers of examples, questions, and clarifications before they're ready to work independently. Mayo frames guided practice not as an innate talent but as a teachable, improvable instructional skill, comparable to questioning and checking for understanding, that strengthens through deliberate practice. The piece promises practical strategies for strengthening this lesson phase specifically.
points: Identifies guided practice ('We Do') as one of the hardest parts of explicit teaching to execute well.
Notes there's no fixed script for guided practice — it must adapt in real time to how each class responds.
Frames guided practice as requiring constant observation, response, and in-the-moment instructional decisions.
Reassures teachers that guided practice is a learnable skill, not an innate talent, improvable through deliberate practice.
Positions guided practice alongside questioning, modelling, and checking for understanding as a core explicit-teaching skill.
quotes: Have you ever wondered whether you're getting the 'We Do' phase right? You're not alone.
Guided practice is arguably one of the most challenging parts of an explicit teaching lesson to deliver well.
Unlike modelled instruction or independent practice, there isn't a script to follow. Every lesson is different because every group of students responds differently.
That's what makes guided practice such a sophisticated teaching skill. It requires teachers to constantly observe, respond and make instructional decisions in real time.
The good news is that guided practice isn't something you're either naturally good at or not.
Like questioning, modelling and checking for understanding, it's an instructional skill that becomes stronger with deliberate practice.
